title: How Long Does Alcohol Stay in Urine? EtG and Urine Test Windows
excerpt: How long alcohol shows up in a urine test: standard ethanol tests vs the EtG "80-hour" test, cutoff levels, what changes the window, and false positives.
metaDescription: Alcohol shows in a standard urine test for about 12 hours, and an EtG test can catch it for up to 80 hours. Cutoffs, false positives, and what changes it.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: how long does alcohol stay in urine
content:
**The honest answer first:** it depends on which urine test you mean. A standard urine *alcohol* (ethanol) test usually finds alcohol for roughly 10 to 12 hours after your last drink, sometimes a bit longer after a heavy night. An **EtG** urine test, which looks for a breakdown product of alcohol rather than alcohol itself, is far more sensitive. It is often advertised as an "80-hour test," and after heavy drinking it can stay positive for about three days, sometimes longer. After one or two drinks, EtG usually falls below common cutoffs within about a day or two, but there is no exact clock that applies to everyone.

**The quick version by test:**

| Urine test | What it looks for | Typical detection window |
|---|---|---|
| Urine ethanol | Alcohol itself | About 10-12 hours after the last drink, longer after heavy drinking |
| EtG (ethyl glucuronide) | A minor metabolite of alcohol | Up to about 24-48 hours after light drinking; up to about 80 hours (3+ days) after heavy drinking |
| EtS (ethyl sulfate) | A second minor metabolite, usually tested alongside EtG | Similar to EtG, often slightly shorter |

These are typical ranges reported in toxicology references and lab guidance, not guarantees. The amount you drank, your body size, your kidney function, how concentrated your urine is, and the **cutoff level** the lab uses all move the number. The rest of this guide explains each of those so you can understand a result instead of guessing at it.

> **This is general information, not legal or medical advice.** If a urine alcohol test affects your job, a court case, custody, or a medical treatment plan (such as a transplant list), ask the program or lab directly what test and cutoff they use, and tell them in advance about any medicines or products you use that contain alcohol. **See a doctor or get urgent care if** you notice blood in your urine, pain or burning when you pee, very dark urine that doesn't clear with fluids, or pain in your back or side after drinking. **If you drink heavily every day and get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you stop** (for example, while stopping before a test), that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor before stopping suddenly. Call 911 for confusion, seizures, or hallucinations.

## How Your Body Gets Rid of Alcohol (and Why Urine Only Sees a Little of It)

To understand urine tests, it helps to know where alcohol actually goes.

After you drink, alcohol is absorbed from your stomach and small intestine into your blood, and it spreads through all the water in your body. From there:

- **The liver handles almost all of it.** Enzymes called alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase turn alcohol into acetaldehyde and then into acetate, which your body eventually breaks down into carbon dioxide and water. This accounts for the vast majority of the alcohol you drink.
- **A small amount leaves unchanged.** A few percent leaves your body as plain alcohol in your breath, sweat, and urine. That is what breathalyzers and urine ethanol tests measure.
- **A tiny fraction becomes EtG and EtS.** Well under 1% of the alcohol you drink is attached to other molecules in the liver to form ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and ethyl sulfate (EtS). These by-products are harmless, but they hang around in urine much longer than alcohol itself, which is why they are useful to testers.

The liver works at a fairly steady pace. On average, blood alcohol falls by about 0.015 g/dL per hour, which works out to roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults. That rate varies from person to person, and you cannot meaningfully speed it up with coffee, water, exercise, or a cold shower. (Our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) goes through what does and doesn't help.)

This matters because the two kinds of urine test are measuring very different things. An ethanol test asks "is alcohol still in your body right now?" An EtG test asks "has your body processed alcohol recently?"

## How Long Does Alcohol Show Up in a Standard Urine Test?

A urine ethanol test measures alcohol itself. Because alcohol is cleared from the blood within hours, this kind of test has a short window: usually around 10 to 12 hours after your last drink.

A few details explain why the window is a little longer than your blood alcohol:

- **Urine sits in your bladder.** Urine made while your blood alcohol was high can stay in your bladder until you pee. So a sample can still contain alcohol for a while after your blood alcohol has dropped to zero. Emptying your bladder once and testing a later sample gives a more current reading, which is why some programs ask for a second sample.
- **Heavy drinking extends it.** If your blood alcohol peaked very high, it takes your liver longer to work through it, and urine stays positive longer. After a very heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood the next morning, not just your urine.
- **Urine lags behind blood.** Urine alcohol tends to rise and fall a little later than blood alcohol, so it reflects the recent past rather than this exact moment.

Urine ethanol tests are used less often these days for monitoring, because a negative result only tells you someone hasn't had alcohol in the last half-day or so. Programs that want to know about the last few days use EtG instead.

## How Long Does Alcohol Stay in Urine for an EtG Test?

EtG is the test most people are worried about when they search this question. It is used by courts, probation programs, professional monitoring programs (for nurses, doctors, pilots and similar), some workplaces, and transplant teams.

### Why EtG lasts so much longer

EtG is only made while alcohol is in your body, but once it's made, it is cleared by the kidneys more slowly than alcohol is cleared by the liver. So it keeps showing up in urine for a day or more after the alcohol itself is gone. That's the whole point of the test: it catches drinking that a breathalyzer or urine ethanol test would miss.

### Typical EtG windows

The often-quoted figure is that EtG can be found **up to about 80 hours** after drinking. That upper end usually applies to heavy drinking. Here is how the window generally scales, based on published research and lab guidance:

- **One or two drinks:** EtG is often detectable for roughly 12 to 24 hours, and sometimes up to about two days at sensitive cutoffs.
- **A moderate night out (several drinks):** often around one to three days.
- **Heavy drinking or a binge:** often three days or more, and occasionally longer, especially at a low cutoff.

These overlap a lot, because individual results vary. Two people who drank the same amount can test differently.

### Why "80 hours" isn't a promise either way

The 80-hour number is a ceiling that shows up in marketing and summaries, not a fixed timer. It doesn't mean every drink is detectable for 80 hours, and it doesn't mean you are guaranteed to be clear at hour 81 after a very heavy weekend. The cutoff level, how much you drank, and how diluted your sample is all change where your result lands.

## EtG Cutoff Levels: The Part That Decides Your Result

An EtG test doesn't just say "yes" or "no" to any trace at all. Labs use a **cutoff**, a concentration above which the result counts as positive. Cutoffs are reported in nanograms per milliliter (ng/mL). The most common ones are 100, 500, and 1,000 ng/mL.

The US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) published an advisory on alcohol biomarkers that offered a rough guide to reading EtG levels. In general terms:

- **Above 1,000 ng/mL ("high positive"):** suggests heavy drinking on the same day or the day before, or drinking within the last day.
- **500 to 1,000 ng/mL ("low positive"):** may reflect heavy drinking in the past one to three days, recent light drinking, or recent heavy exposure to alcohol-containing products.
- **100 to 500 ng/mL ("very low positive"):** may reflect heavy drinking one to three days ago, light drinking in the past day, or incidental exposure.

The key takeaway is that **lower cutoffs catch more, including things that aren't drinking.** A 100 ng/mL cutoff is very sensitive. It can pick up light drinking well into the next day, and it is also the range where heavy use of hand sanitizer, mouthwash, or other products can sometimes register. A 500 ng/mL cutoff is a common middle ground used by many programs to reduce false alarms from incidental exposure.

If you are in a testing program, it is completely reasonable to ask what cutoff they use. That one number does more to explain a result than anything else.

## What Affects How Long Alcohol Stays in Your Urine?

The biggest factors, roughly in order of importance:

1. **How much you drank.** More alcohol means more EtG made and a longer time before it falls under the cutoff. This is by far the most important variable.
2. **How recently you drank.** EtG levels peak several hours after drinking and then decline. A sample taken the next morning will usually be higher than one taken two days later.
3. **How concentrated your urine is.** Urine that's very concentrated (first thing in the morning, or when you're dehydrated) shows higher EtG levels. Very dilute urine shows lower ones. Labs know this, which is why many measure creatinine (a natural waste product) to judge whether a sample is too dilute to trust.
4. **Kidney function.** EtG is cleared by the kidneys. People with reduced kidney function can have EtG in their urine for longer than usual.
5. **Body size, sex, and body water.** These affect how high your blood alcohol gets from a given number of drinks, and so how much EtG you make. Women and smaller people usually reach a higher blood alcohol from the same drinks, partly because they have less body water.
6. **Individual metabolism.** People simply vary in how much EtG they produce from the same dose of alcohol. Research on EtG has consistently found wide differences between people.

Things that **don't** meaningfully change the window: coffee, saunas, exercise, cranberry juice, "detox" drinks, or niacin. None of these make your liver or kidneys clear alcohol metabolites dramatically faster.

## Does Drinking Water Flush Alcohol Out of Your Urine?

Not really, and trying can backfire.

Water doesn't speed up how fast your liver breaks down alcohol, and it doesn't make your body produce less EtG. What it does do is **dilute** your urine. A very dilute sample may show a lower EtG concentration, but it doesn't make the alcohol history disappear.

Testing labs and programs are well aware of this. Many check:

- **Creatinine**, to see if the sample is unusually dilute.
- **Specific gravity**, another measure of concentration.

A sample flagged as dilute is often treated as invalid or suspicious, and many programs treat a dilute or tampered sample the same way as a positive one, or require a retest under observation. So trying to "flush" before a test can create more trouble than it solves.

Staying normally hydrated is still good for you after drinking, because it helps with how you feel, even if it doesn't change the test. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) covers the recovery timeline and where fluids help.

## Can You Fail an EtG Test Without Drinking?

Yes, at low cutoffs it is possible, which is one reason SAMHSA advised against using a single EtG result on its own to make serious decisions about someone.

EtG is made whenever ethanol enters your body, whether you drank it or not. Common sources of incidental exposure include:

- **Alcohol-based hand sanitizer**, especially frequent heavy use, mainly through breathing in the vapor and some absorption through the skin.
- **Mouthwash** that contains alcohol.
- **Medicines** that contain alcohol, such as some liquid cough and cold syrups.
- **"Non-alcoholic" beer and wine**, which in the US can legally contain up to 0.5% alcohol. Drinking a lot of it can produce low-level EtG results.
- **Cooking extracts** like vanilla extract, and to a lesser extent kombucha, which can contain small amounts of alcohol.

In most cases, normal use of these products produces EtG levels well below a 500 ng/mL cutoff. The risk is higher with a 100 ng/mL cutoff and with heavy or unusual use.

There are also lab-side issues. EtG can, in some situations, be produced or broken down in the urine sample itself by bacteria, for example in a sample from someone with a urinary tract infection. That's one reason many labs test for **EtS** at the same time: EtS is more stable and isn't affected by bacteria in the same way. A positive EtG with a negative EtS is a result worth questioning.

**If you're in a testing program,** the practical steps are:

- Ask which products the program wants you to avoid. Many give a list (hand sanitizer, mouthwash, cough syrups, non-alcoholic beer).
- Switch to alcohol-free mouthwash and soap-and-water handwashing while you're being tested.
- Tell the program in writing about any alcohol-containing medicines you need.
- If a result surprises you, ask whether EtS was tested and whether the result was confirmed with a lab method (usually LC-MS/MS) rather than only an initial screen.

## Can a Urine Test Show How Much You Drank?

Only roughly. A urine EtG level can suggest whether drinking was light or heavy and whether it was recent, which is how the SAMHSA ranges above are framed. But it can't give you an exact number of drinks, because the result depends on so many things: timing, urine concentration, body size, and individual metabolism.

A urine ethanol test is even less precise about quantity. Because urine pools in the bladder, the alcohol level in urine doesn't line up neatly with your blood alcohol at the moment of testing. That's why legal blood alcohol readings come from blood or breath, not urine.

## Urine vs Breath, Blood, Saliva, and Hair Tests

Urine tests sit in the middle of the detection range. Here's how they compare with other common alcohol tests:

| Test | What it measures | Typical window |
|---|---|---|
| Breathalyzer | Alcohol in breath (reflects blood alcohol) | While alcohol is still in your blood, usually up to about 12-24 hours depending on how much you drank |
| Blood alcohol | Alcohol in blood | Similar to breath: hours, up to about a day after heavy drinking |
| Saliva | Alcohol in saliva | Roughly 12-24 hours |
| Urine ethanol | Alcohol in urine | About 10-12 hours, longer after heavy drinking |
| Urine EtG/EtS | Alcohol metabolites | About 1-3 days; up to about 80 hours after heavy drinking |
| Blood PEth | Phosphatidylethanol, a marker formed in red blood cells | Up to a few weeks after repeated drinking |
| Hair EtG | EtG stored in hair | Up to about 90 days, depending on hair length |

If you want a deeper comparison of the long-window tests, our guide to [PEth vs EtG alcohol testing](/never-hungover/peth-vs-etg-alcohol-testing-advanced-biomarker-comparison-guide-2025) explains how blood PEth differs from urine EtG, which one is used for what, and how their results are interpreted.

## Quick Timeline: What a Urine Test Might Show After a Night Out

To make this concrete, here's a rough picture for a typical adult who had about four or five drinks over an evening and stopped at midnight. Treat it as an illustration, not a prediction.

- **Midnight to early morning:** blood alcohol is still elevated. Breath, blood, and urine ethanol tests would all likely be positive.
- **The next morning (8 to 10 hours later):** blood alcohol may be near zero or gone. A urine ethanol test could still be positive, especially from the first urine of the day. EtG is likely high.
- **The next evening (about 18 to 24 hours):** urine ethanol is very likely negative. EtG is very likely still positive at common cutoffs.
- **Day two to day three (about 48 to 72 hours):** EtG may have dropped below a 500 ng/mL cutoff, but could still show up at a 100 ng/mL cutoff.
- **After about three to four days:** EtG would usually be below common cutoffs for this amount of drinking, though heavier drinking pushes the whole timeline later.

The more you drank, the further every one of these points shifts to the right.

## When to See a Doctor

Most people searching this question are just curious or have a test coming up. But some urine changes after drinking are worth a medical opinion. See a doctor if you notice:

- **Blood in your urine**, or urine that looks pink, red, or cola-colored.
- **Pain or burning when you pee**, or needing to go very often with little coming out. That can mean a urinary tract infection, which can also affect test results.
- **Very dark urine that doesn't lighten** after you drink normal fluids, especially with yellowing of your skin or eyes. That can be a sign of a liver problem.
- **Pain in your back or side**, just below the ribs, after drinking.
- **Peeing much less than usual** for a day or more.

And if you are a heavy daily drinker who needs to stop before a test, please don't do it alone and abruptly. **Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, nausea, or trouble sleeping when you stop drinking can be signs of alcohol withdrawal,** and severe withdrawal can cause seizures or confusion. A doctor can help you stop safely. Confusion, seizures, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there is an emergency: call 911.

## Can Anything Help Your Body Process Alcohol?

The honest answer is that your liver sets the pace, and the only reliable way to have less alcohol and EtG in your urine is to drink less, drink more slowly, or not drink before a test. No supplement, drink, or trick will clear a urine test, and you should be wary of any product that claims it can.

What you can do is make the drinking you choose to do easier on your body. Eat before and while you drink, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and give yourself time to recover afterward.

Some people also take supplements to support how they feel after drinking. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best described as promising rather than proven. **There is no good evidence that DHM shortens how long alcohol or EtG shows up in your urine, and it will not help you pass an alcohol test.** If you want to try it for how you feel the next day, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- A standard urine alcohol test usually finds alcohol for about 10 to 12 hours after your last drink, longer after heavy drinking.
- An EtG urine test is much more sensitive. It usually picks up light drinking for about a day or two and heavy drinking for up to about 80 hours, sometimes longer.
- The lab's **cutoff level** (often 100, 500, or 1,000 ng/mL) has a huge effect on the result. Lower cutoffs catch more, including some incidental exposure.
- Drinking extra water dilutes urine but doesn't clear alcohol faster, and labs check for dilute samples.
- Hand sanitizer, mouthwash, medicines, and non-alcoholic beer can produce low-level EtG. If you're being tested, avoid them and tell the program about anything you need to use.
- See a doctor for blood in your urine, pain when peeing, or dark urine that won't clear, and talk to one before stopping if you drink heavily every day.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How long does alcohol stay in your urine?**

A standard urine ethanol test usually detects alcohol for about 10 to 12 hours after your last drink, and longer after heavy drinking. An EtG test, which looks for a breakdown product of alcohol, can detect drinking for about one to three days, and up to about 80 hours after heavy drinking.

**How long does one drink stay in your urine?**

After a single standard drink, a urine ethanol test would usually be negative within several hours. An EtG test may still pick it up for roughly 12 to 24 hours, and sometimes up to about two days if the lab uses a sensitive 100 ng/mL cutoff.

**Will drinking water help me pass an EtG test?**

No. Water doesn't make your body clear EtG faster. It only dilutes your urine, and labs check creatinine and specific gravity to spot dilute samples. Many programs treat a dilute sample as a failed or invalid test.

**Can hand sanitizer cause a positive EtG test?**

It can, at low cutoffs and with heavy use. Alcohol-based sanitizer can produce small amounts of EtG, mostly from breathing in the vapor. At a 500 ng/mL cutoff, normal use is unlikely to cause a positive result, but at 100 ng/mL it's possible. If you're being tested, switch to soap and water.

**Is an EtG test the same as an 80-hour test?**

Yes, "80-hour test" is a common nickname for the EtG urine test. The 80 hours is an upper estimate that usually applies to heavy drinking. Light drinking is often undetectable well before that, and very heavy drinking can occasionally be detected longer.

**Does a urine test show how drunk you are?**

No. Urine pools in your bladder, so the alcohol level in urine doesn't match your blood alcohol at the moment of the test. Blood or breath tests are used for that. A urine EtG result can suggest whether drinking was recent and heavy or light, but not exactly how much you drank.

**Can DHM help me pass a urine alcohol test?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how long alcohol or EtG stays in your urine. Your liver and kidneys set that pace. DHM is studied for how people feel after drinking, not for avoiding detection.
